title: Heathrow expansion: jobs, costs, climate and local impact
label: 14 October 2026 · Heathrow expansion evidence
summary: Heathrow’s CEO and Chief Development Officer told the committee they believe a third runway is essential for UK trade, jobs and inward private investment, and that most key costs and mitigations are included in their plans. MPs probed affordability, who pays for rail and other access, the planning timetable (now showing 2039 as the likely opening), how independent oversight would work, and whether climate, noise, biodiversity and local compensation are properly covered. Heathrow stressed its modelling and mitigation plans but accepted uncertainty on timing, some regulatory decisions and questions about long-term carbon and community impacts.

speakers.label: Helen Elsby
speakers.name: Helen Elsby
speakers.role: Chief Development Officer, Heathrow Airport Ltd.

glossary.definition: Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement — the government policy document that guides planning decisions for the runway project.
Development Consent Order — the legal permission a big infrastructure project needs to build and operate.
Civil Aviation Authority — the UK regulator that approves airport investment and checks affordability for airlines and passengers.
Air Passenger Duty — a tax on air tickets that raises money and can affect ticket prices.
Sustainable Aviation Fuel — lower-carbon aviation fuels that can cut emissions but are currently limited and costly.
Ultra-fine particles — tiny airborne particles measured around airports that may affect health but currently lack UK limits.
Department for Transport — the government department responsible for transport policy and some funding decisions.
Judicial review — a court process that can delay or challenge a planning decision.
The accounting framework the CAA uses to decide which airport investments earn a return through regulated charges.

chapters.title: Why Heathrow says expansion matters to the whole UK
chapters.takeaway: Heathrow argues a third runway draws large private investment, boosts trade and creates jobs nationwide; the committee probed how much is new growth versus displacement.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why is Heathrow expansion critical for national growth, and does the HENPS reflect that?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: Heathrow brings large private investment and national benefits: billions in extra GDP (we've modelled figures up to about £17bn), roughly 108,000 extra jobs in 20 years, and thousands of apprenticeships. The hub role can't be replaced by other UK airports.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Supporters cite better connections from regional airports to Heathrow, but higher slot costs may make regional flights uneconomic. How does that stack up?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: We price to encourage domestic feeder flights—short haul is cheaper than long haul. Amsterdam shows hubs can keep regional connections viable. Competition among airlines and the market will determine exact outcomes.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: You say freight will increase. Is that new production or cargo switching from sea (which is lower carbon) to air?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: The growth is exporters expanding because they can reach new markets—medical, light manufacturing, fresh foods. Consultants and universities we commissioned modelled those trade effects.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: DFT modelling suggested displacement of activity toward west London rather than net UK growth. Does that weaken the national-growth case?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: DFT's model treats the investment as taxpayer money and misses some trade and private-investment effects. It also assumes Heathrow competes with regional airports; in practice we complement them, which regional airports themselves accept.

chapters.title: Costs and affordability: who pays and when
chapters.takeaway: Heathrow says £33bn–£35bn is privately financed and includes mitigation and surface access elements; MPs pushed on whether airlines, passengers or government bear extra costs and on testing affordability.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You warned investors might go elsewhere if runway 3 doesn't proceed. Isn't that capital mobile and able to fund other UK projects?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: Investors could put money elsewhere, but I don't know of any other project of Heathrow's scale with equivalent nationwide benefits; our investors haven't said they have alternative plans of that size.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should affordability be a formal test in the HENPS?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: Affordability is vital. But we already have ongoing cost control through the CAA regulator—every pound we spend is pre-approved. Making affordability a one-off planning test risks duplicating or undermining the CAA's role.

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: We agree affordability must be checked continuously during the 20-year delivery. We want regular ‘touchpoints’ and independent assurance through the project life, not a single pass/fail at planning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does the advertised £33bn–£35bn include noise mitigation, surface access and carbon costs such as SAF?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: Yes. The figure covers the expansion elements, mitigation we believe the policy requires, surface-access elements proportionate to airport benefits, and other known scope. We built contingencies into the cost plan.

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: To put it in perspective, airport users already pay about £30 in APD; our estimate for the runway adds roughly £15 per passenger in capital terms, though airlines recover costs through fares in different ways.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Several airlines oppose the project as unaffordable. Do they agree with your definition of affordability?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: We are aligned with airlines on the need for affordability. We regularly discuss cost reductions with them and seek to agree the best balance to deliver benefits without making the scheme unaffordable.

chapters.title: Timetable, delivery risks and independent oversight
chapters.takeaway: Heathrow now plans a 2039 opening for the runway rather than 2035, citing planning and investor constraints; they support joint assurance but stress past delivery experience.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: Reports say the opening date slipped from 2035 to 2039. What changed?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: We always modelled a range of scenarios. 2035 was an ambitious target; planning reforms and pre-consent commitments to buy land didn't materialise. Investors prefer committing large sums after consent, so we've re-phased some pre-consent activity and now plan for 2039 as our robust case.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: Does that push terminal upgrades and full capacity later too?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: Yes—phasing moves. T5X (a new terminal west of T5) and some linked works shift in line with the runway. We still safeguard improvements so modernisation can continue without expansion consent, but later phases follow the runway timing.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: How do investors feel about that slippage?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: Investors want regulatory clarity and a credible business case more than a fixed date. The key missing elements are the final HENPS and the CAA's long-term regulatory model; once those are clear investors will decide.

turns.speaker: Steff Aquarone
turns.text: Would you welcome clearer milestones and independent oversight written into HENPS?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: Yes. We already have airline oversight of spend; we propose a joint assurance board with independent experts, airlines and Heathrow to improve transparency and efficiency on delivery.

turns.speaker: Steff Aquarone
turns.text: What are the biggest delivery risks—things outside your control?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: Land acquisition timescales and interfaces with highways (like the M25), local facilities and potential legal challenges (JR) are risks. Technically it's feasible—moving roads and rivers has been done—but complexity and delay are the main threats.

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: We delivered Terminal 5 on time and on budget and have experience of large M25 works. We use standard risk registers, independent assurance and contingencies as part of our cost plan.

chapters.title: Surface access and who pays for rail and roads
chapters.takeaway: Heathrow says it includes some rail and landside measures in its cost plan but expects to fund only the airport-specific share; larger rail links may need other promoters or government funding.

turns.speaker: Daniel Francis
turns.text: Does the £27bn for terminals and infrastructure include surface access costs? How much are you planning to spend?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: Our cost plan includes a comprehensive landside package: passenger interchanges, road upgrades (including M25 changes), walking and cycling routes and elements of rail infrastructure that directly benefit Heathrow passengers.

turns.speaker: Daniel Francis
turns.text: Who pays for the big rail links further afield—southern or western links into Heathrow?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: We fund the proportionate airport benefit. Wider rail benefits for the country would need other funders or a different promoter. We are talking to DFT and potential promoters about how a larger rail scheme could be funded and delivered.

turns.speaker: Daniel Francis
turns.text: How will the DCO enforce modal share targets—getting people onto public transport?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: HENPS should state clear mode-share targets. In a DCO application we must show how we'll meet them; consent conditions can make those outcomes legally enforceable if granted.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The 2018 ANPS said landside traffic shouldn't be greater than today. Is that commitment still in force?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: We're moving from a single prescriptive test to outcome-based mode-share metrics in the HENPS. We'll be held to the new targets and must demonstrate how we meet them.

chapters.title: Climate, air quality, noise and biodiversity
chapters.takeaway: Heathrow says it has modelled carbon over the project life and has mitigation levers (SAF, new aircraft, airspace changes, carbon capture), but MPs pressed on post‑2050 emissions, grid power for electrification, UFPs and biodiversity risks.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: You asked for clearer climate-test methodology. Have you modelled emissions beyond 2050, since expansion finishes after then?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: Yes. We've modelled the scheme's carbon over its life and believe there is a credible path to meet HENPS carbon tests, drawing on multiple levers: SAF uptake, more efficient aircraft, airspace improvements and carbon removal technologies—but we need supportive policies and mandates.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: Isn’t that risky—relying on technologies or fuels that are not yet available at scale?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: Some elements are proven—new aircraft and SAF exist now (we load several percent daily). The risk is scale and policy support, not technical proof of concept. We need mandates and supply to ramp up.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does Heathrow face a grid power constraint for electrifying ground equipment and vehicles?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: Current analysis says we have enough power for the next decade. We have applied for a new direct grid connection expected by 2037; we'll confirm where the power will come from and follow up with the Committee.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are you measuring ultra-fine particles (UFPs) and could increased SAF use or new evidence on UFPs create local air-quality problems?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: We measure particles, including UFPs, frequently. UFP science is evolving and there are currently no UK thresholds. If evidence shows harm, limits and mitigation would be required. We'll work with regulators on that.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Your sustainability appraisal shows higher biodiversity risk because the scheme is bigger. How will you leave nature better?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: We manage a large nature estate already and aim to deliver at least a 10% net biodiversity gain. We publish nature reports, and expansion gives an opportunity to improve habitats if we co-design with environmental bodies.

chapters.title: Local communities, noise mitigation and compensation
chapters.takeaway: Heathrow stresses the toll of long uncertainty on local residents and says compensation measures are in the NPS, but MPs sought detail on take-up, enforceability and whether standards should be in the NPS or DCO.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Local people have lived with 20 years of uncertainty. What should happen for them now?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: A timely decision is important so communities can move on. The chosen scheme was selected to minimise housing loss and noise over London; that balance matters.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: You said you spend £14m a year on noise mitigation—how many people actually uptake that help?

turns.speaker: Thomas Woldbye
turns.text: I don't have the exact uptake figure to hand—it's in the low hundreds; we'll write to the Committee with the precise number.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should specifics of community compensation be set in the NPS or in the DCO?

turns.speaker: Helen Elsby
turns.text: We think the NPS should set outcome-based thresholds and some high-level commitments (house purchase uplift is already in the NPS). The DCO and consent conditions should set the technical delivery details so they are enforceable.
